chapter: Introduction — The Greatest Show on Earth
idea: Money outcomes depend more on behavior than knowledge — on how people act with what they know, not what they know.
application: When plans drift toward optimizing tooling instead of consistent behavior, name the gap: the compounding lever is habits, not hacks.

idea: Everyone's money decisions make sense from inside their own experience — people are shaped by what they've lived through.
application: When reviewing someone else's priorities or your own past choices, assume a coherent reason existed; update the model, don't just update the judgment.

idea: Not all success is hard work, and not all poverty is laziness — outcomes mix effort with luck and risk outside your control.
application: When the weekly review compares trajectories, evaluate decisions by process quality, not just outcomes; one bad outcome isn't one bad process.

idea: Know what 'enough' is: moving the goalposts' satisfaction ceiling never arrives by earning more alone.
application: Bigger-ticket goals (promotion, side project) need named finish lines — undefined ambition creates tasks that can never be completed.

idea: Compounding's power is its consistency over long time — not intensity; uninterrupted streaks beat heroic bursts.
application: Protect streak mechanics (daily review, weekly briefs) — restarting from zero costs more than skipping intensity ever saves.

idea: Getting there and staying there are different skills: survival mindset — longevity and flexibility — beats maximizing returns.
application: Balance the matrix: shipping 100% growth projects leaves no slack; keep some resilience margin (buffer tasks) for surprises.

idea: In fields driven by tails, most outcomes are ordinary and a few carry everything; breadth of attempts buys lottery tickets cheaply.
application: For interviews and projects, increase the number of small attempts (problems tried, demos shipped) rather than perfecting one bet.

idea: The highest dividend money and career pay is control over your time — the ability to do what you want, when you want.
application: Guard calendar whitespace: meetings filling the whole schedule are directly trading away career's best dividend; keep unplanned hours.

idea: People buy status to get admiration, but observers mostly see the object, not the owner — they imagine themselves in it.
application: Prefer impact-metrics over visibility-metrics in reviews: contributions judged by what changed for others, not what ceremony it had.

chapter: 9. Wealth is What You Don't See
idea: Wealth is discretion — the unbought options, the untaken hours; flashy spending converts hidden slack into visible liabilities.
application: Value the quiet stuff in plans: prepared environments, unspent scope, untouched buffer — these are the 'wealth' of the schedule.

idea: Saving without a goal builds optionality; savings rate is the only variable fully in your control.
application: Keep a standing 'optionality' block per week — uncommitted focus time whose whole job is absorbing whatever opportunity hits.

idea: Be reasonable, not maximally rational: a strategy you can actually live with beats one you'll abandon.
application: Match study/work loads to what the user will actually sustain — 45 focused minutes daily beats a heroic schedule abandoned by Thursday.

idea: History is the study of surprises: we plan around past patterns while the future's biggest moves are unprecedented ones.
application: Plans should carry explicit 'what if this is wrong' branches for high-stakes goals, not just optimistic single-path timelines.

idea: Build room for error — the gap between what could happen and what will happen is where plans die.
application: Any plan adjacent to real deadlines gets buffer time attached (planner suggests 90-min blocks; leave deliberate gaps).

idea: You will change your mind about what matters; don't over-commit to a trajectory today that your future self will pay to exit.
application: Revisit priorities in the weekly review before adding new long-horizon tasks; avoid stacking commitments you may outgrow quietly.

idea: Every upside has a price that often shows up as effort, volatility, or failure along the way — treat these as fees, not flaws.
application: Hard problems that get attempted and failed weekly ARE the tuition for interview readiness; don't cancel study plans after bad sessions.

idea: Bubbles and trends are games with different players and different rules — know which game you're actually in before copying others.
application: When adopting shiny practices (new stack, new method), ask which constraint differs between that player and you.

idea: Pessimism sounds smarter and travels faster than progress, but it's usually noise around slowly improving reality.
application: In weekly reviews, weight the slow positive trend lines (attempts logged, streaks kept) over dramatic setbacks when composing narrative.

idea: Beliefs get welded to incentives and stories; appealing narratives outperform accurate ones — especially about the future.
application: Ground every summary in real numbers from the data; when numbers are missing, say so instead of dressing a story in confident language.

idea: The strategy summary: keep options, tune behavior, avoid ruin, credit luck, and let consistency do the heavy lifting.
application: Use this lens when proposals cross domains: which option improves optionality and which just adds motion.
